metaDescription: Own minerals in Washington County? We buy Marcellus and Utica interests directly, explain your division order in plain English, and close on your timeline.
heroLead: My grandfather signed his first gas lease in Washington County back when a well was just a curiosity on the back forty. Now it's the wettest, busiest part of the whole Marcellus play, and the mail still shows up confusing.
intro: Washington County sits at the center of the Marcellus wet-gas window, and it has for over a decade. Range Resources drilled some of its earliest Pennsylvania pads here, and EQT, CNX, and a handful of smaller operators followed. If your family holds minerals anywhere between Canonsburg and California, Claysville and Charleroi, there's a decent chance a horizontal well has already crossed under your ground, or a unit line has swept through it, whether a rig ever sat on your own surface or not.

That density is exactly why Washington County owners end up with some of the most confusing royalty statements in the state. Pooled units, allocation wells, deducted post-production costs, an interest that got split four ways in a will from 1987 and never got cleaned up at the recorder of deeds. We've bought minerals across this county for years, and we still see a new statement every week that would take a landman a full afternoon to untangle.

sections.heading: Why Washington County Draws So Much Drilling Interest
paragraphs: Washington County isn't a fringe county in the Marcellus play, it's close to the heart of it. The rock here runs thick and rich in natural gas liquids, which is why operators pay more attention to a lease here than they do thirty miles north where the gas turns dry. Ethane and propane content in the wet-gas window means a well here can be worth drilling even when Henry Hub prices sag, because the liquids carry their own separate value.

That's part of why lease and unit activity never fully stopped here the way it did in some drier counties during the 2015-2016 downturn. Companies kept permitting, kept pooling new units, kept coming back for infill wells on pads that had already produced for years. If you inherited an interest here, odds are good it's tied to a unit that's actually active, not sitting dormant waiting on a pipeline that may never come.

sections.heading: The Post-Production Deduction Fight Owners Are Still Fighting
paragraphs: Pennsylvania's Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act sets a floor of one-eighth, but it doesn't say a word about what an operator can deduct before that eighth ever gets calculated. Gathering, compression, dehydration, transportation to the sale point, marketing fees, they all get taken off the top on a lot of older Washington County leases, and the Kilmer v. Elexco decision from the state Supreme Court gave operators room to do exactly that as long as the lease language allows it. We've had sellers hand us a royalty statement showing a gross value on one line and a net check for barely half of it, and the confusion on their face is the same look my own family had the first time it happened to us.

If your lease was signed before anyone in your family thought to ask a landman about a no-deduction clause, you're probably living with that math every month. It's one of the biggest reasons owners here decide to sell rather than keep watching costs eat into a check that should be bigger.

sections.heading: Act 13 Impact Fees and What They Actually Mean for You
paragraphs: Act 13 set up an impact fee system in 2012 that sends unconventional well fees to counties and municipalities, and Washington County has collected some of the largest impact fee distributions in the Commonwealth because it hosts so many producing wells. That money pays for roads, emergency services, and local infrastructure, but it's a fee paid by the operator to local government, not a royalty paid to you as the mineral owner. We mention it because a lot of owners hear impact fee on county budget news and assume it has something to do with their own check. It doesn't, and understanding that distinction helps you read your own statement more clearly instead of chasing numbers that were never yours to begin with.

sections.heading: How a Sale Works if You Own Minerals Here
paragraphs: We start with your deed and your most recent division order, run the parcel against active units and permits filed with the Pennsylvania DEP, and give you a straightforward cash offer based on what's actually producing or reasonably likely to be developed. There's no pressure to sign fast and no vague promise of a number we can't back up. Some families sell everything, others keep a piece and sell the rest to cover a specific need. We close through a title company, the same way any real estate transaction in Washington County closes, and we handle the recorder of deeds paperwork ourselves.

faqs.question: How do I know if my Washington County minerals are held by production?
faqs.answer: Check your lease's habendum clause and compare it against permits and unit filings on the DEP's oil and gas mapping tool. If a well within your unit has been producing, most standard leases stay held by production indefinitely. We can walk you through this at no cost before you decide anything.

faqs.question: Do you buy interests that aren't currently leased?
faqs.answer: Yes. Unleased minerals in an active area like Washington County still carry value because a future operator will eventually need to lease or pool them. The value is different than a producing, leased interest, but it's rarely zero.

faqs.question: Will selling affect the impact fee money the county collects?
faqs.answer: No. Act 13 impact fees are paid by the operator based on the well, not tied to who owns the mineral interest underneath it. Selling your minerals has no effect on county or municipal impact fee revenue.

faqs.question: What if my deed only covers a fractional interest?
faqs.answer: That's common in Washington County, especially on land that's passed through several generations. We buy fractional and undivided interests regularly and can explain exactly how your percentage translates to value.

faqs.question: Do I need a lawyer to sell my mineral rights?
faqs.answer: It isn't required, but for larger or more complicated interests we always encourage owners to have their own attorney review the purchase agreement. We're happy to work alongside whoever you choose.
